name: Hot hand fallacy
statement: The belief that a basketball player who has just made several shots is more likely to make the next one was declared a cognitive illusion in 1985.
meaning: Two separate claims travel under one name, and keeping them apart is the whole story. The first is about players: that a run of hits raises the chance of the next hit. The second is about observers: that the run tells them nothing, so believing in it is an error of reasoning. Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky argued the first was false and the second therefore true. The name of the entry belongs to the second claim. It survives only for as long as the first one fails.

origin.who: Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky
origin.note: Their paper is "The hot hand in basketball: On the misperception of random sequences". They found no dependence between successive shots and concluded that the widespread belief in streak shooting was, in words Miller and Sanjurjo quote from page 313, "a powerful and widely shared cognitive illusion".

evidence: Three datasets and two surveys, described by Tversky and Gilovich in Chance in 1989. For nine Philadelphia 76ers across 48 home games of the 1980-81 season, the chance of a hit was .51 after a hit and .54 after a miss, with eight of the nine players shooting better after a miss. Free throws for nine Boston Celtics over the 1980-81 and 1981-82 seasons showed no dependence between the first shot and the second. In the controlled experiment, 14 men and 12 women from the Cornell varsity teams each took 100 shots from a distance where they made about half, giving .47 after a hit and .48 after a miss, with a mean serial correlation of .02. One of the 26 produced a significant positive correlation, r = .37, which the authors put down to chance. Against that, a sample of 100 avid fans from Cornell and Stanford was near unanimous: 91% said a player has a better chance after making his last two or three shots, and for a hypothetical 50% shooter they put the figure at 61% after a make and 42% after a miss. A separate group of 100 knowledgeable fans judged sequences of 21 hits and misses, and classified a perfectly random one as streak shooting 65% of the time. The 1985 paper is closed at Elsevier and had no open copy at Unpaywall or Semantic Scholar when this was checked, so the figures above are read off the authors' own 1989 account; Miller and Sanjurjo reproduce the Cornell table from the raw data.

replication.headline: The 1985 finding of no hot hand did not survive: the statistic it rested on is biased downwards, and correcting it reverses the result.
replication.detail: Miller and Sanjurjo proved in Econometrica in 2018 that the proportion of successes on the trials following a streak of successes is a biased estimator of the underlying probability, even for a fair coin. Selecting the trials that follow a streak is a selection rule, and it favours sequences in which those trials are failures. The bias grows with streak length and shrinks with sequence length, and it is large at the sizes the literature uses. For a shooter taking 100 shots with a fixed 50% chance, the expected gap between shooting after three hits and after three misses is not zero but minus 8 percentage points. Gilovich and colleagues' Cornell players averaged .49 after three hits and .45 after three misses, a paired t-test on which Miller and Sanjurjo reproduce at p = .49. Correcting each player's difference for the bias implied by his or her own shooting percentage and shot count moves the average from +3 to +13 percentage points, with a standard error of 4.7 points and p < .01. Nineteen of 25 players then point the right way, and five reach individual significance. Permutation tests, which carry no bias by construction, agree at p < .01. Other streak lengths are weaker: +10 points at four hits, which does not reach 5% at p = .07 one-sided, and +5.4 points at two, p < .05 one-sided.

study.cite: Miller, J. B., & Sanjurjo, A. (2018). Surprised by the hot hand fallacy? A truth in the law of small numbers. Econometrica, 86(6), 2019-2047.

limits: The correction is arithmetic and nobody disputes it. How much hot hand the corrected data show is another matter. Ritzwoller and Romano rebuilt the analysis on permutation tests, which carry no bias by construction, and rejected random shooting in the Cornell data at streak lengths of two and three, p = .040 and p = .004 on the difference statistic. Drop one shooter, who began by missing nine in a row and later made 16 in a row, and only the streak-of-three test still clears 5%. Their power calculations say the four controlled shooting experiments are too small to detect streakiness of the size that variation in NBA field goal percentages would imply. The shooting contests give a warmer reading. Miller and Sanjurjo report in Econometrica that 28 years of NBA Three-Point Contest data, covering 33 players with at least 100 shots, give an average bias-corrected difference of +8 percentage points, p < .01, with 8 of the 33 individually significant. Lantis and Nesson took the 1986-2019 contests apart by shooting location in 2024 and found the effect only within a location: making the previous shot raised the next by 5.2 to 5.9 points, while the first shot after moving showed about two points in the wrong direction and no significance. Game data has not settled either. Lantis and Nesson, over 12 NBA seasons, found a small hot hand in free throws and none in field goals, where longer streaks of makes lowered the chance of the next one. Mews and Ötting modelled 110,513 NBA free throws in continuous time and found a hot hand raising success by a few percentage points. Pelechrinis and Winston, using optical tracking of about 200,000 shots a season across two seasons and 153 players with at least 1,000 shots, found 24 players with a hot hand after one make and 41 after four, while the league-wide adjusted effect ran the other way at minus 1.4 to minus 2.7 percentage points. Miller and Sanjurjo also report that a close replication of the Cornell study by Avugos and colleagues reverses on correction, though the authors declined to supply the raw data and the figures come from the published table.
misreadings: The overturning is about the evidence, not about basketball. The verdict at the top of this page is about the 1985 finding, which did not survive retesting. It is not a ruling that players never get hot, and the two claims point in opposite directions. What collapsed is the 1985 inference, because the test used to reach it cannot come out at zero under its own null hypothesis. That is a property of the estimator, not a coding error or a selective report, and it went unnoticed for three decades by people checking the arithmetic. Reading the reversal as proof that players get hot also goes further than the data. The clearest evidence sits in controlled shooting and in the three-point contest, where sample sizes are small enough that a single streaky player moves the result. Two large in-game studies of field goals report no positive league-wide effect: Lantis and Nesson found none over 12 seasons, and Pelechrinis and Winston found one running the other way, while naming individual players who do show a hot hand. The second misreading is the mirror of the first. Showing that the belief is not baseless does not show it is calibrated. Fans in 1985 put a 50% shooter at 61% after a make and 42% after a miss, which is a stronger effect than the corrected shooting data show, on a question the survey and the experiment did not pose the same way. Ritzwoller and Romano hold that none of the available estimates of belief are directly comparable to measurements of serial dependence in shooting, and conclude that larger data and more structured elicitation are needed to settle it.
